prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Wife and servant are the same, But only differ in the name: For when that fatal knot is tied, Which nothing, nothing can divide: When she the word obey has said, And man by law supreme has made, Then all that’s kind is laid aside, And nothing left but state and pride: Fierce as an Eastern prince he grows, And all his innate rigour shows: Then but to look, to laugh, or speak, Will the nuptial contract break. Like mutes she signs alone must make, And never any freedom take: But still be governed by a nod, And fear her husband as a God: Him still must serve, him still obey, And nothing act, and nothing say, But what her haughty lord thinks fit, Who with the power, has all the wit. Then shun, oh! shun that wretched state, And all the fawning flatt’rers hate: Value your selves, and men despise, You must be proud, if you’ll be wise.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Wife, But, For

outputs.L1:
Wife and servant are the same,  
Differing only in the name;  
For when that fatal knot is tied,  
Which nothing—nothing—can divide,  
When she has spoken the word “obey,”  
And man is made supreme by law,  
Then all that once was kind is cast aside,  
And nothing remains but status and pride.  

Fierce as an Eastern prince he grows,  
And all his innate severity shows;  
Then merely to look, to laugh, or speak  
May seem the nuptial contract to break.  
Like mutes, she must communicate by signs alone,  
And never claim a freedom of her own;  
Still governed only by his nod,  
And taught to fear her husband as a god.  

Him she must serve, him she must obey,  
And neither act nor speak in any way  
Except as her haughty lord thinks fit—  
He who, possessing power, claims all the wit.  

Then shun—oh, shun—that wretched state,  
And hate all fawning flatterers;  
Value yourselves, and men despise:  
You must be proud, if you would be wise.
outputs.L2:
A wife is treated no differently from a servant; the distinction lies only in the title. Once the marriage bond is fastened—one that is meant never to be broken—and once she has promised to “obey,” the law places the man above her. From that moment, tenderness disappears, and rank and arrogance take its place.

He becomes as harsh and commanding as an absolute ruler, revealing all his natural severity. A mere glance, a laugh, or a word from her may be treated as a violation of the marriage agreement. She is expected to communicate only by silent gestures, like someone forbidden to speak, and to claim no liberty for herself. She must be ruled by the slightest sign from him and fear her husband as though he were a god.

She is required always to serve him, always to submit to him, and neither do nor say anything unless her proud master approves it. Since he holds all the authority, he assumes he also possesses all the wisdom. Therefore, avoid—yes, avoid—that miserable condition, and distrust those who flatter you into accepting it. Respect your own worth and look down on men’s pretensions; if you want to be wise, you must also be proud.
outputs.L3:
The speaker argues that marriage reduces a wife to the status of a servant rather than an equal partner. In the poem, marriage is presented not as a loving union but as an institution that gives men power over women. Once a woman becomes a wife, she is expected to submit to her husband’s authority and surrender much of her independence.

Husbands are portrayed as becoming tyrannical after marriage because the law gives them control over their wives. The poem suggests that men may appear charming and affectionate before marriage, but once they have legal power, they often use it to dominate. Marriage therefore becomes a trap in which the husband’s authority is protected and the wife’s freedom is restricted.

The wife is described as losing her freedom of speech, action, and self-expression. She can no longer speak openly, act according to her own wishes, or present herself as an independent individual. Instead, she must regulate her behaviour to please her husband and avoid his disapproval. Her identity is diminished because her thoughts, choices, and desires are subordinated to his.

The husband is also portrayed as demanding obedience and reverence as if he were a god. He expects his wife not only to obey him but also to honour and admire him unquestioningly. This comparison highlights the excessive and unjust nature of male authority within marriage, showing how the husband’s role becomes inflated into something almost divine while the wife is treated as inferior.

As a result, the speaker warns women to avoid marriage, value themselves, and reject the flattering words of men. The poem encourages women to recognise their own worth and to be cautious of romantic promises that may conceal future oppression. Rather than surrendering their freedom for the illusion of love, women are urged to protect their independence and resist a system that turns them into servants.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a sharp critique of marriage, portraying it not as a romantic partnership but as a system that reduces women to servants within their own homes. Through stark comparisons and satirical warnings, the speaker exposes how marriage can strip wives of freedom, dignity, and independence. Rather than gaining security or happiness, women are shown as entering a “wretched state” in which they must obey husbands who hold legal, social, and domestic power over them. The poem challenges the idealized view of marriage by revealing the inequality hidden beneath promises of love and protection.

A central concern of the poem is the loss of female autonomy. Once married, a woman is expected to surrender her own will and submit to her husband’s authority. The poem suggests that marriage gives men control over women’s lives, making wives dependent on their husbands and forcing them into roles of service and obedience. This critique is especially powerful because it attacks not only individual men, but the broader social system that allows men to dominate women. Marriage is presented as an institution that normalizes inequality and teaches women to accept subordination as their duty.

The poem also warns women against being deceived by flattering suitors. Men may use charm, praise, and promises of affection to persuade women into marriage, but the speaker suggests that such attention often hides the reality of control and confinement that follows. By using satire, the poem mocks the false language of courtship and exposes the dangers behind it. Women are encouraged to see through romantic illusions and recognize their own worth before giving up their independence.

Ultimately, the poem’s key message is that women should value themselves and be cautious of a social order that asks them to trade freedom for marriage. It urges women to reject obedience as their natural role and to resist a system that treats them as inferior. By presenting marriage as a condition that can deprive women of autonomy, the poem becomes a powerful argument for female self-respect, independence, and awareness of the injustices built into traditional gender relations.
outputs.L5:
My wife is my closest friend and strongest supporter. She brings warmth, patience, and laughter into every day. But like any relationship, marriage takes effort, understanding, and honest communication. There are moments of disagreement, but they can become opportunities to grow closer.

For a happy life together, love must be shown not only through words, but also through actions. Small gestures, respect, and kindness can make a relationship stronger over time. A wife is not just a partner in daily life; she is someone to cherish, support, and appreciate.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical 17th-century-style poem warning women against marriage, comparing a wife’s condition to that of a servant.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Warning to Maids, Touching Matrimony**

Come hither, maids, and lend an ear,  
Whilst I in sober jest appear;  
If Hymen’s torch you needs must try,  
First mark what smoke attends it nigh.  

A wife, though deck’d in bridal lace,  
Doth oft but change her name and place;  
The ribband fades, the garland dies,  
And household chains in order rise.  

For when the parson’s work is done,  
And two, they say, are made but one,  
The reck’ning commonly is clear:  
The husband’s one, the wife’s cashier.  

She rises ere the cock hath crow’d,  
To sweep, to brew, to bear the load;  
She mends his hose, she warms his meat,  
And learns to smile at sour conceit.  

If he come home with cloudy brow,  
She must not ask the where or how;  
If he be merry, she must laugh;  
If drunk, must hold the stirrup-staff.  

The servant hath her wage at night,  
And may, perchance, dispute her right;  
But wives, for all their daily pain,  
Are paid with “peace, good wife,” again.  

The maid may quit a churlish place,  
And seek a kinder master’s grace;  
The wife, once bound by law and bed,  
Must serve till she or he be dead.  

Her keys may jingle at her side,  
Yet little kingdom doth she guide;  
For he that buys the beef and beer  
Will be the lord and overseer.  

Then pause, fair maids, ere vows be said,  
And weigh the pillow with the bread;  
For love is sweet in songs and rings,  
But marriage hath a thousand strings.  

Yet if you wed, let wisdom stand  
Beside your heart and hold your hand:  
Choose not a master for your life,  
But one that knows a wife’s no wife  

Unless she be, in house and name,  
A friend, not fuel for his flame;  
Else better keep your maiden key  
Than gilded servitude to see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhymed feminist poem in archaic English about how marriage makes husbands tyrannical and wives powerless.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Ballad of the Wedded Yoke**

O list, ye maids, and mark my rede,  
Ere vows be bound and rings be tied;  
For oft the rose that brides do heed  
Is thorn’d when set by husband’s side.  

He comes with honey on his tongue,  
With “sweeting mine” and courtly grace;  
Yet when the marriage-bell is rung,  
A lordly mask o’ershades his face.  

“Obey,” quoth he, “for thou art mine;  
Thy will shall wither under me.”  
Thus love, that seem’d a thing divine,  
Is chain and lock and iron key.  

Her purse he shuts, her path he bars,  
Her speech he weighs, her friends he bans;  
He names his whims for holy stars,  
And calls his hunger Heaven’s plans.  

She, once a falcon wing’d and fair,  
Must fold her pinions in his hall;  
Must breathe by leave, and eat by prayer,  
And smile when he hath stolen all.  

If she should cry, “My heart is sore,”  
He saith, “Peace, wife; thy grief is sin.”  
If she should seek the open door,  
He bolts the world and keeps her in.  

O marriage, made a golden crown,  
How oft thou turn’st to bridle-bit;  
How oft thy silken veil falls down  
To blind the eyes that burn through it.  

Yet mark me well: no wife is clay  
For any man’s remoulding hand;  
Her soul was wrought ere wedding-day,  
And answereth not to his command.  

Rise, sisters, rise from hearth and chain;  
Let no false lord your daylight dim.  
For love that liveth by your pain  
Is love no more—but death in trim.  

And if a husband would be true,  
Let him be mate, not magistrate;  
For hearts are twain, and wills are two,  
And neither born to serve as fate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Restoration-era verse monologue advising women to avoid matrimony and value their own freedom.
counterfactuals.output:
Ladies, attend: let not the gilded snare,  
Call’d Marriage, catch your unsuspecting hair.  
A ring!—a pretty toy to please the eye,  
Yet mark what chains beneath its lustre lie.  
The priest may smile, the bridegroom bow and swear,  
But oaths grow thin as smoke in common air.  

To-day he kneels, all flame, all sigh, all art;  
To-morrow claims the empire of your heart.  
Your fan, your friends, your walks, your very thought,  
Must all be tax’d, and to his audit brought.  
He calls it love to rule, and care to spy,  
And bids you thank him when he clips your sky.  

What is a husband? Oft a household king,  
Whose crown is temper, and whose sceptre—sting.  
If kind, you’re bound to praise his generous chain;  
If sour, you must endure, and not complain.  
Your wit must sleep, lest it outshine his own;  
Your mirth must ask permission ere ’tis shown.  

But single life!—there blooms the nobler state:  
No tyrant hour, no lordly “soon” or “late.”  
Your mornings yours, your evenings unbetray’d,  
Your purse unplunder’d and your will obey’d.  
You choose your books, your visits, and your dress,  
Nor purchase shelter with a soul’s distress.  

Let fools for settlements their freedom sell,  
And call a cage, if finely wrought, a cell.  
Let mothers preach, and grave relations chide:  
“Secure your fortune—be some man’s fair bride.”  
A fortune? Say rather, hazard, debt, and strife—  
The dice-box of a whole uncertain life.  

Keep, then, your hearts from contract and from cage;  
Be mistresses of youth, of wit, of age.  
Love, if you must, as sovereigns grant a grace,  
Not as poor captives suing for a place.  
For she who weds may wear a silken gown,  
Yet oft has pawn’d her liberty for a crown.  

Stand free, bright nymphs; let no fond bargain prove  
That bondage is the proper end of love.  
The world will call you proud—why, let it see  
A woman may be proud, and still be free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem in the style of early modern women writers, with heroic couplets criticizing the word “obey” in marriage vows.
counterfactuals.output:
**Against “Obey”**

When sacred hands in mutual faith are tied,  
Let neither soul be humbled for a bride;  

For Love, that noble guest, will never stay  
Where one must command and one obey.  

If Heaven made two to bear one common name,  
Why should the wife receive a servant’s claim?  

No charter sealed above, no holy breath,  
Ordains her living liberty to death.  

The vow that makes one heart of two allied  
Should set no throne upon the husband’s side.  

For she who yields from tenderness alone  
Gives more than force could ever make its own.  

But “obey”—that iron syllable—would prove  
A chain set ringing in the house of love.  

It turns the altar to a judgment-seat,  
And lays a crown beneath another’s feet.  

Let prudence guide, let sweet consent command,  
And both walk equal, hand enclosed in hand.  

Then marriage shall not be a gilded cage,  
Nor custom’s law the scripture of an age;  

But souls, by choice and mutual honor led,  
Shall keep one vow, where neither bows the head.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an old-fashioned anti-marriage poem beginning with the idea that “wife and servant are the same” and ending by urging women to despise men.
counterfactuals.output:
I can write it as an old-fashioned, satirical anti-marriage poem critiquing patriarchal husbands and unequal marriage—without urging hatred of men as a whole.

**A Spinster’s Counsel**

Wife and servant are the same,  
When marriage makes a lordly claim;  
One wears a ring, one wears a chain,  
Yet both must rise and toil again.  

She darns his hose, she pours his tea,  
She bends where once her thoughts flew free;  
Her wages paid in “dearest wife,”  
Her pension but a faded life.  

He calls her angel, hearth, and dove,  
Then taxes every proof of love;  
He praises softness, meek and mild,  
And keeps her poorer than a child.  

O maidens, mark the bargain well:  
A gilded cage is still a cell.  
Keep purse, keep key, keep heart, keep hand,  
Nor bow to any man’s command.  

If marriage come with equal grace,  
With mutual honor, room, and place,  
Then choose it freely, if you can—  
But scorn the tyrant, not the man.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
